title: Network & Wi-Fi
blurb: No internet, slow or dropping Wi-Fi, can't see other computers.

remedies.title: Wi-Fi says connected, but nothing loads
remedies.why: The computer reached the Wi-Fi box but not the internet beyond it. Usually the router or internet line is down, the computer kept an old address, or a VPN or proxy is in the way.

steps.text: Run the Network doctor: it checks Wi-Fi, the router, name lookup and the internet in turn and tells you which link is broken.
Check another device (a phone on the same Wi-Fi). If it has no internet either, restart the router: unplug it for 30 seconds, plug it back in and wait 2–3 minutes.
Turn Wi-Fi off and on again on this computer.
Clear the computer's list of remembered website addresses.
If you use a VPN or a proxy, turn it off and try again.
If you use a VPN, disconnect it and try again; check Network settings for a proxy you don't expect.
Still nothing: reset the network settings (needs a restart).

remedies.escalate: If other devices work and this one doesn't after a reset, tell IT what the Network doctor reported and whether a VPN or security app is installed.

remedies.title: Wi-Fi keeps dropping or disconnecting
remedies.why: Weak signal, interference from other networks, power saving turning the Wi-Fi card off, or an old Wi-Fi driver.

steps.text: Move closer to the router, or away from microwaves, thick walls and metal. If the router has separate 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz names, try the other one.
Forget the network and join it again: Settings › Network & internet › Wi-Fi › Manage known networks › Forget.
Forget the network and join it again: Wi-Fi settings › the ⓘ next to the network › Forget This Network.
Stop Windows turning the Wi-Fi card off to save power: Device Manager › Network adapters › your Wi-Fi adapter › Properties › Power Management › untick "Allow the computer to turn off this device".
Update the Wi-Fi driver from the PC maker's support site (or Windows Update › Optional updates).
Run Wireless Diagnostics (hold Option and click the Wi-Fi icon › Open Wireless Diagnostics) to see interference and signal.
Restart the router; if it's several years old or drops for every device, it may need replacing.

remedies.escalate: Tell IT whether it happens to every device or only this one, in which room, and roughly how often.

remedies.title: Internet is slow
remedies.why: Weak Wi-Fi signal, something else using the connection (updates, cloud sync, other people streaming), or the internet plan itself.

steps.text: Run a speed test close to the router, then where you usually sit. A big drop means the Wi-Fi signal, not the internet.
Pause big uploads and downloads: cloud backup, OneDrive/iCloud/Dropbox sync, game or system updates.
Check what's using the network: Task Manager › Processes › sort by Network.
Check what's using the network: Activity Monitor › Network tab, sort by Sent/Received.
Use the 5 GHz network if your router has one; it's faster at short range.
Plug in a network cable if you can; if it's fast on the cable, the problem is Wi-Fi coverage.
Restart the router. If speeds are still far below your plan on a cable, call your internet provider.

remedies.escalate: Give IT or the provider the speed test results (on cable and on Wi-Fi) and the time of day.

remedies.title: My Wi-Fi network doesn't show in the list
remedies.why: Wi-Fi or airplane mode is off, the network is hidden or 5 GHz-only on an older card, or the Wi-Fi adapter is switched off.

steps.text: Make sure airplane mode is off and Wi-Fi is on.
Make sure Wi-Fi is on in Control Center or Wi-Fi settings.
Check that other devices see the network. If none do, restart the router.
If the network is hidden, add it by name: Wi-Fi › Manage known networks › Add network.
If the network is hidden, use Wi-Fi settings › Other… (at the bottom) and type its name.
Some laptops have a Wi-Fi key or switch (often Fn + a key with an antenna icon); press it.
Check the Wi-Fi adapter is enabled: Network Connections › right-click Wi-Fi › Enable.

remedies.escalate: If no networks show at all and the adapter is missing from Device Manager, the Wi-Fi hardware or driver has failed: tell IT the computer model.

remedies.title: The Wi-Fi option is gone completely
remedies.why: Windows can't see the Wi-Fi adapter: its driver failed after an update, it's disabled, or (rarely) the hardware failed.

steps.text: Restart the computer fully: Start › Power › Restart (not Shut down; fast startup can keep the problem).

Open Device Manager › View › Show hidden devices › Network adapters. If the Wi-Fi adapter has a down arrow, right-click › Enable device. If it has a warning sign, right-click › Uninstall device, then restart.
Reset the network settings (needs a restart).
Install the Wi-Fi driver from the PC maker's support site using another computer or a cable.

remedies.escalate: Tell IT the computer model and whether the adapter appears in Device Manager.

remedies.title: Wi-Fi says the password is wrong (but it's right)
remedies.why: The computer remembers an old password, the password was changed on the router, or Caps Lock / keyboard layout is changing the letters.

steps.text: Check Caps Lock and the keyboard language (a different layout can swap letters like Y and Z or symbols).
Forget the network, then join it again and type the password fresh.
Forget the network, then join it again and type the password fresh.
On a Mac, an old saved password can also live in Keychain Access: search for the network name and delete the entry.
Ask whoever runs the router whether the password changed. Work networks may need a username as well, not just a password.

remedies.escalate: For a work network that asks for a username, IT has to check your account or certificate.

remedies.title: Work Wi-Fi asks about a certificate or keeps asking to sign in
remedies.why: Work and school networks check your account (and often a certificate) every time. A changed password or an expired certificate stops it working.

steps.text: If you changed your work password recently, forget the network and join again with the new password.
Only accept a certificate if IT told you to expect it; a fake network can show one too.
Check the date and time are right: a wrong clock makes certificates look expired.
Check the date and time are set automatically.
Use the guest or setup network your workplace provides to install their Wi-Fi profile, if they have one.

remedies.escalate: IT needs to check your account and the network's certificate; tell them the exact message.

remedies.title: Network cable plugged in, but no connection
remedies.why: A loose or damaged cable, a dead wall port, a USB/dock adapter that isn't working, or the computer preferring a different connection.

steps.text: Check both ends of the cable click in, and that the light by the port blinks. Try another cable and another port on the router or wall.
If you use a dock or USB network adapter, unplug it and plug it back in; try it on another USB port.
Check Ethernet is enabled: Network Connections › right-click Ethernet › Enable.
Check the Ethernet service in Network settings and its status; for a USB adapter, see that it's listed.
Run the Network doctor to see which link fails.
Reset the network settings (needs a restart).

remedies.escalate: Tell IT which wall port number you used and whether a laptop works on the same cable.

remedies.title: One website won't load, others do
symptoms: server ip address could not be found
remedies.why: The site may be down, or the computer remembers an old address for it. Browser extensions and security software can also block single sites.

steps.text: Try the site on your phone using mobile data. If it fails there too, the site itself is down: wait a while.
Try a private window (it skips extensions and old cookies).
Clear the computer's address cache.
Restart the Mac or turn Wi-Fi off and on to clear the address cache.
Turn off a VPN, ad blocker or web filter for a moment and try again.

remedies.escalate: Tell IT the exact address and error message, and whether it works on your phone.

remedies.title: Shared drive or network folder disappeared
remedies.why: The computer isn't on the work network (or VPN), the server is down, or your saved login for the server is out of date.

steps.text: If you're away from the office, connect the VPN first; shared drives only work on the work network.
Open the drive in File Explorer; a red X often clears when you click it once it can reach the server.
If you changed your password, update the saved one: Credential Manager › Windows Credentials › the server's entry › Edit (or Remove, then reconnect).
Reconnect: Finder › Go › Connect to Server (⌘K) and type the address IT gave you (smb://server/share).
If you changed your password, delete the old server entry in Keychain Access and reconnect.
Make sure the network is marked Private on Windows (Public hides the PC and blocks sharing).

remedies.escalate: Give IT the server or drive path and the exact error; check whether coworkers can reach it.

remedies.title: Can't see other computers or share files on the home network
remedies.why: Windows hides this PC and blocks sharing on networks marked Public.

steps.text: Set the network to Private: Settings › Network & internet › your network › Private network.
Turn on network discovery and file sharing: Network & internet › Advanced network settings › Advanced sharing settings.
Reach the other computer by name or address directly: in File Explorer's address bar type \\computername or \\192.168.1.20.

remedies.escalate: On a work network, sharing is often blocked on purpose; ask IT.

remedies.title: "IP address conflict" or "self-assigned IP"
remedies.why: The router didn't hand this computer an address (169.254… is a stand-in), or two devices were given the same one.

steps.text: Turn Wi-Fi off and on (or unplug and replug the cable) to ask for a new address.
Restart the router; it hands out the addresses.
Reset the network settings (needs a restart).
Network settings › your connection › Details › TCP/IP › Renew DHCP Lease.
If someone set a fixed address on this computer, set it back to automatic (DHCP) unless IT asked for it.

remedies.escalate: Tell IT the address shown and whether other devices on the same network get online.

remedies.title: Can't connect to my phone's hotspot
remedies.why: The hotspot switches itself off after a while, the phone's plan blocks tethering, or the computer remembers an old hotspot password.

steps.text: Keep the phone's hotspot screen open while connecting; many phones hide it when idle.
On iPhone turn on "Maximize Compatibility" in Personal Hotspot; on Android try the 2.4 GHz band.
Forget the hotspot on the computer and join again.
Check your phone plan includes hotspot use.
Try USB tethering with the phone's charging cable instead.

remedies.title: Internet only works with the proxy off (or a proxy appeared)
remedies.why: A proxy routes web traffic through another server. One left over from work, a VPN, or unwanted software breaks browsing.

steps.text: Open proxy settings. Unless IT set one up, turn off "Use a proxy server" and setup scripts; keep "Automatically detect settings" on.
Network settings › your connection › Details › Proxies: turn off proxies you didn't set up.
If it comes back by itself, check for unwanted software (see Security).

remedies.escalate: On a work computer, the proxy may be required; ask IT before removing it.
